h1: The 6 Best Microwaves With Large Displays of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 countertop microwaves scored on capacity, wattage, sensor cooking and footprint, from 0.9 to 2.2 cubic feet.
summary: The TOSHIBA 2.2 Cu. Ft. with smart sensor is the best microwave overall, with the largest cavity and 1200W. The GE 1.6 is the balanced pick, the Farberware 1.6 is best for auto-cook presets, and the BLACK+DECKER 0.9 is the compact choice. Display size is not published on these listings, so confirm the readout in photos.
intro: When a buyer wants a microwave with a large display, the real wish is simple: read the time without squinting and press the right button without hunting. Spec sheets rarely say how big the numerals are, which means readability is the one thing you have to check yourself in photos and reviews.

This ranking covers six countertop microwaves. We reviewed their listings for capacity, power, sensor cooking and footprint, since those are published, and we flag the display as a check item rather than guess at its size. Pair that with owner photos before you order.

products.name: TOSHIBA 2.2 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave with Smart Sensor
products.verdict: The roomiest and most powerful microwave here, with a smart sensor that takes guesswork out of reheating.
products.description:
This Toshiba is a 2.2 cubic foot countertop microwave rated at 1200W with a smart sensor. It is the biggest chamber and the highest wattage in the group, which means a full dinner plate or a large casserole dish can turn without hitting the walls.

It takes first place because capacity and power are the two numbers that change daily life most, and a sensor means the oven adjusts time by itself rather than leaving you to read the clock. The tradeoff is physical size and cost: it sits in the $200 to $500 bucket and needs a counter or cabinet footprint much larger than the other picks. The listing does not publish display dimensions, so confirm the readout by looking at owner photos.

Buy it if you cook for a family or reheat big dishes and want one microwave to handle everything. Skip it if counter space is tight. Measure the spot first, and leave ventilation clearance around the back and top.
products.idealFor: Families who reheat large plates and want sensor cooking.
products.skipIf: Your counter or cabinet space is limited.

products.name: GE 1.6 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1150W, 1.6 cubic foot GE that balances capacity and counter footprint.
products.description:
GE lists this countertop model at 1150W with a 1.6 cubic foot chamber. The combination is a sweet spot for most households: enough room for a 12-inch dinner plate and enough power to heat dense leftovers evenly.

It ranks second because it matches the Farberware 1.6 on capacity and beats it on listed wattage, while costing less than the Toshiba 2.2. The tradeoff versus the top pick is raw volume, and the listing offers few feature details beyond the two numbers. Verify the control panel in photos, since the display is what this guide is about.

Buy it if you want a mid-size microwave from a brand with wide service coverage. Skip it if you want a sensor on the listing. Its listing falls in the $100 to $200 range.
products.idealFor: Most households wanting power without a giant footprint.
products.skipIf: You want sensor cooking listed in the specs.

products.name: Farberware 1.6 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1100W Farberware with smart sensor auto-cook settings and a defrost mode.
products.description:
The Farberware 1.6 is listed at 1100W with smart sensor auto-cook settings and a defrost function. Sensor cooking measures steam from the food and adjusts the cycle, which is handy for popcorn, potatoes and frozen meals.

It ranks third because it has the feature list of the Toshiba 2.2 at a lower tier, but its power sits slightly below the GE. The tradeoff is that the extra auto programs add menu depth, so a person who wants fewer buttons may find the panel busier. The listing falls in the $100 to $200 range.

Buy it if you like pressing a food button and walking away. Skip it if you prefer manual timing. Check owner photos for the control panel and display readability before ordering.
products.idealFor: Cooks who like preset food buttons and sensor cooking.
products.skipIf: You want the simplest possible controls.

products.name: TOSHIBA 1.2 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1000W, 1.2 cubic foot Toshiba for kitchens that do not need a big cavity.
products.description:
Toshiba lists this countertop model at 1.2 cubic feet and 1000W. That is a common mid-size configuration, large enough for most mugs, bowls and a standard plate.

It ranks fourth because it offers fewer headline features than the picks above and a smaller chamber than the 1.6 models, but it keeps a firm 1000W rating. Its edge is a more compact body, so it is easier to place in a dorm, an office kitchen or a small apartment. The tradeoff is the narrower interior, which struggles with large dishes. The listing falls in the $100 to $200 range.

Buy it if you want a trustworthy mid-size unit. Skip it if you regularly heat big casserole dishes. Confirm the display and key layout in photos, since the listing does not describe them.
pros: Easier to fit on small counters
products.idealFor: Small kitchens and offices that want a capable mid-size oven.
products.skipIf: You heat large plates or casseroles often.

products.name: Farberware 1.3 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 1000W Farberware with auto-cook settings and defrost at a modest price.
products.description:
This Farberware lists 1000W, a 1.3 cubic foot cavity, auto-cook settings and defrost. It is a smaller sibling of the 1.6 model and offers a similar set of food presets.

It ranks fifth because the cavity is a bit larger than the Toshiba 1.2 but the listing lacks the sensor wording of its bigger sibling, and it sits behind both on power-to-size ratio. The tradeoff is that auto-cook here means timed presets rather than steam sensing. The listing falls in the $100 to $200 range.

Buy it if you want presets in a small body. Skip it if you want a true sensor. Inspect photos of the display, since readability depends on the panel layout.
products.idealFor: Apartment cooks who want presets in a compact oven.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 0.9 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 900W, 0.9 cubic foot microwave for dorms, desks and small kitchens.
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER is a 0.9 cubic foot countertop microwave rated at 900W. It is the smallest model in this ranking and its listing falls in the $50 to $100 range.

It lands at the bottom since the cavity is small and the power rating is the lowest, but those same traits make it a good fit for a dorm room or a desk. It cannot match the Toshiba 1.2 on capacity or the GE on power. The tradeoff is simply scale: you save money and space by accepting less of both.

Buy it if you heat mugs, bowls and single portions. Skip it if you routinely heat dinner plates. Check the photos of the keypad, since display readability is what sets this guide apart.
pros: Easy fit in dorms and offices
products.idealFor: Students and office kitchens heating single portions.
products.skipIf: You heat full dinner plates or large dishes.

whatMatters.detail: A large, high-contrast readout means you can read the timer from across the kitchen. Because listings rarely give character height, look at owner photos taken from a normal standing distance. Pay attention to whether the numerals are bright and whether the panel is angled.

Capacity is measured in cubic feet, and a 12-inch plate generally needs about 1.4 cubic feet or more to turn freely. A 0.9 or 1.2 oven suits mugs and bowls. Compare the interior dimensions on the listing, not just the cubic-foot number.
More watts heat faster and more evenly. 900W is slow with dense food, while 1100W or higher handles dinner plates quickly. Higher power also costs more, so match it to how often you cook from frozen.
A smart sensor reads steam and stops itself, while a preset runs a fixed time. Sensors are better for variable portions. On a listing, look for the words sensor or humidity, not just auto cook.
A big microwave needs air around its vents. Measure width, depth and height of the space, and leave a few inches at the back and above. A unit that is too tight will run hot and shorten its life.

faq.q: Do these microwaves publish their display size?
faq.a: No. The listings we reviewed give capacity, wattage and cooking features, but not character height. Check owner photos or ask the seller before you buy if readability is your top priority.

faq.q: What mistake do people make buying a microwave?
faq.a: Buying by wattage alone. Interior size, turntable diameter and the control panel decide daily satisfaction, so confirm the cavity fits your plates and that the panel is easy for you to read.

faq.q: Is the Toshiba 2.2 worth it over the GE 1.6?
faq.a: If you heat large dishes or cook for several people, the bigger chamber and sensor are worth the extra. For one or two people the GE does nearly everything and costs less.

faq.q: How do I set the clock and child lock?
faq.a: Most panels use a clock button and a number pad, and a child lock is usually a long press on the stop or lock key. Check the manual, since the sequence varies by brand.

faq.q: How should I clean a microwave?
faq.a: Heat a bowl of water with a splash of vinegar for a few minutes, let it steam, then wipe the walls. Clean spills quickly so they do not bake on.

faq.q: Can I put metal in a countertop microwave?
faq.a: Avoid it. Metal can arc against the cavity walls, so stick to dishes labeled microwave-safe and keep foil clear of the sides.

finalTake: The TOSHIBA 2.2 Cu. Ft. is the best all-round microwave here if you have the space, and the GE 1.6 is the better fit for most kitchens. Because these listings do not state display dimensions, look at owner photos of the panel before you buy, and choose the model whose layout is easiest on your eyes.
